damodaran.quote: the most telegraphed 3rd quarter number of all time
damodaran.summary: On the amendment's Q3 numbers. He values Anthropic at about $1.48 trillion and says he will sit out if it prices well above that; he won't short it.

ritter.quote: a lot of things have to go right
ritter.summary: Only 14 of 4,110 US IPOs from 1980 to 2024 priced above 40 times sales, and they trailed the market by 15.4% on average. A value above $1.4T needs a path to $100B or more of annual after-tax profit.

renaissance_kennedy.quote: I wouldn't say these results are worrisome, but I do expect some of this pressure on growth and margins ... to be reflected in the ultimate IPO valuation
renaissance_kennedy.summary: Q3 isn't alarming, but slower growth and thinner margins should lower the IPO price.

ives.quote: you could call it 1.5, is maybe baseline ... to what probably could even go lower by mid-November.
ives.summary: Still bullish on Anthropic's importance, but sees $1.5T as the baseline for valuation talk and calls an expected junk credit rating a 'gut punch'. Quoted secondhand.

epoch.name: Campbell Hutcheson
epoch.quote: very strong growth, high gross margins
epoch.summary: Paying up for short-term compute is rational; the fundamentals are still strong while the company invests heavily in research.

tunguz.summary: Bull case: 11.9x growth on a derived ~40% gross margin, the first operating profit (~$974M in Q2), positive cash flow and almost no drawn debt. Bear case: $637B of commitments (his sum of the seven named deals in the original S-1), two-thirds non-cancelable, against consumption revenue customers can cut.

add.name: Tony Trzcinka
add.quote: The key question is whether revenue can compound fast enough to absorb the future commitments and outpace compute cost
add.summary: A credit investor's view: the $895.4B of commitments against revenue growth is the crux.

add.name: Brett Winton
add.quote: the frontier lab companies will be good for the bill
add.summary: The world is short of compute, and the leading labs can pay for what they have signed.

0.argument: Revenue went from $41M in 2023 to $33.2B in the first nine months of 2026. Q2 was the first quarter with an operating profit ($974M); Q3 slipped to a $567M loss after a $2.0B non-cash donation charge, for a nine-month operating loss of $1.3B. Operating cash flow was +$6.6B over nine months and adjusted operating income $4.1B (S-1/A pp. 138, 172). Revenue is growing faster than costs.

1.argument: $94.3B of the $104.0B nine-month 2026 net loss, and ~$34B of the $42B 2025 loss, are non-cash fair-value charges on convertible notes, SAFEs and derivatives as the company's value rose. Economically, the operating line and cash flow matter more.

3.argument: Lenders and suppliers (Broadcom, Google) have financed capacity against contracted payments, so financing is not the near-term bottleneck. Anthropic has essentially no drawn debt, a large cash pile and $14.8B available on its revolver.

1.argument: $895.4B of compute commitments as filed in the amendment, of which $213.8B is terminable or conditional (pre-amendment estimates ran $518B–$637B) set against consumption revenue with no lock-in. The payments are owed whether customers stay or not. Rolfes thinks ~70% gross margins are needed to carry them, against ~44% now.

3.argument: ARR is unstandardized and gameable, and Anthropic books cloud-marketplace revenue gross (Damodaran). Nearly half of 2025 sales ran through Amazon and Google, who are also investors, suppliers and competitors. The top five customers were about 25% of nine-month 2026 revenue, though none exceeded 10%. The 2025 cost base was $2.75 per $1 of revenue (Zitron).
